title: Born in Memphis; father the college professor, move to Chicago
summary: Born in Memphis, the family moves to Chicago when he is four or five; his father taught at Le Moine College and is honored there around 1927.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: You were born where?
Memphis, Tennessee. And my family moved

to Chicago. My father was a professor, an English professor, you know, at Le Moine (PHONETIC) College in Memphis. In fact he taught Jimmy Lunceford English, before Lunceford went to Fisk University in Nashville. And then we moved to Chicago when I was, oh, maybe five, four or five, right around the kindergarten stage.
What do you remember from Memphis?

Nothing. Not at that age. But when I went back, and they gave my father kind of a homecoming, and the faculty there, you know. I'll tell you, the most impressed thing that really got to me was the -- it was highly integrated then.
In Memphis?
Yeah.
Tennessee?
Yeah. I was only nine years old then, and my father -- well, the old man was a great student at Fisk, and --
Was that where he graduated from?

Uh-huh. And he went back and they treated him like a king. And that's the only thing I remember, other than the one time I worked with Sarah Vaughan, and of course I have a lot of relatives there. One was a school principal and the other one was a school teacher. You know, that was the thing in those days.
Now are you talking about the time
your father was honored at Fisk or at Le Moine?
No, at Le Moine.
At Le Moine.
Yeah. The faculty there.
And that was when you were nine, so that would be about 1927.
Yeah, just before the Depression hit.
Uh-huh.

And I remember how nice people were. It was a great experience. And the old man was proud to take me around and show me off, you know. And I really didn't know that he was a violin player. I knew he was a choir director. And when he passed all he had mainly was a bunch of big scores. "The Hallelujah Chorus," and those standard things of years ago, you know?
